Concept 03

Pipeline

A Pipeline is a Dataset, the systems that operate on it, and the stage plan SACI derives from what those systems declare. You add systems in an order; SACI works out which of them can share a stage.

In one line
Data plus systems plus the plan derived from both
You need
Nothing beyond saci. ParallelSystem stages, source and sink need the engine feature, which is on by default
Read this if
You have written a few systems and want to know what order they will run in, and what happens to the batch when one of them fails

What a Pipeline holds

Five things. SACI derives the fourth; you fill the rest:

  • A name: Arc<str>, for logs and for the scheduler's dependency graph.
  • A Dataset: the columnar data this workload owns, reached through data() and data_mut().
  • A Vec of systems, held in the order you registered them.
  • One OnceLock holding the derived plan: the stage buckets, the expanded access metadata, and one RetryMode per system.
  • With the engine feature, per-component sources and sinks.

You never build the plan. It is a pure function of the systems you added and the schemas they declare against, computed the first time it is needed.

Building one

A pipeline is a consuming chain: each method takes the pipeline and returns it. component registers a component on the pipeline's dataset, resource inserts a resource, and system adds a system. Rows go in afterwards through data_mut().

Rustconstruct, then add systems in order
use saci::prelude::*;

let mut pipeline = Pipeline::new("etl")
    .component::<Transaction>()           // register a Component
    .resource(Report::default())           // insert a Resource
    .system(ValidateSystem)
    .system(EnrichSystem)
    .system(LimitSystem)
    .system(ReportSystem);

pipeline.data_mut().append::<Transaction>(&seed)?;

schema(name, schema) registers a component whose schema is known only at run time. A registration that fails is held, and validate(), plan() and every run call return it before anything else.

parallel_system takes a ParallelSystem instead: a system that reads an immutable Dataset and returns a WriteSet. That variant is what lets two systems in one stage execute at the same time. It needs the default engine feature. A build without it registers the system, then refuses it at run time, because the sequential executor has no thread pool to give it. system_boxed and parallel_system_boxed take a system that is already boxed.

From declarations to stages

Every system's meta() names the component fields it reads and writes. SACI walks those declarations, adds an edge for every pair that conflicts on a field, and buckets systems by their longest path from a root. The buckets are the stages.

a field some system writes systems, edges, the derived plan

A stage is a guarantee about ordering, not a promise of concurrency

Two systems sharing a stage means only that nothing orders them relative to each other. No field or resource conflict was found, so either order is correct. That guarantee licenses running them at the same time. Acting on the licence is a separate decision.

The executor makes it per stage, from what the stage's members are and how many rows the dataset holds:

The stageHow it executesRetries wait with
Every member impls ParallelSystem, there are 2 or more, and the dataset holds at least STAGE_INLINE_THRESHOLD rows (100_000)Concurrently. One blocking task per system; all are awaited, then the WriteSets merge and apply oncestd::thread::sleep
Every member impls ParallelSystem, and there is exactly 1Directly, then its WriteSet is appliedtokio::time::sleep
Any member is a plain System, or the stage is all-parallel but under the row thresholdOne at a time, in ascending index order. A plain System mutates the Dataset in place; a ParallelSystem has its WriteSet applied as soon as it returnstokio::time::sleep

So a stage of four plain Systems runs strictly one after another, and no wall clock time is saved. Below the row threshold an all-parallel stage runs that way too. One spawn_blocking per system plus the write-set merge costs more than the work it spreads, and stage-mates conflict on nothing, so the result is identical either way. The plan still proved they do not interfere, which is what makes them safe to reorder, to slice, or to hand to a ParallelSystem rewrite later. All three branches accumulate into the same retries total.

The rules, for a system A registered before a system B. Field keys are (component, field) pairs; resource keys are TypeIds.

CaseA declaresB declaresEdge
Read after writewrites Freads FA → B
Write after writewrites Fwrites FA → B
Write after readreads Fwrites FA → B
Read after readreads Freads Fnone
Resource, after a writewrites Rreads or writes RA → B
Resource, write after readreads Rwrites RA → B

reads_all::<C>() and writes_all::<C>() expand to every field in C's registered schema when the plan is built, so they conflict with anything that touches C at all. Declare fields individually when you want two systems to share a stage. reads_all_named and writes_all_named take the component name as a string.

Validation is plan construction

validate() runs no analysis of its own. It builds the same plan a run builds, against the pipeline's own SchemaRegistry, and keeps it, so a successful validate() leaves plan() readable and makes the first run() free of plan work. Anything it catches is exactly what run() would have caught first:

  • A declared read or write naming a component that is not registered.
  • A declared read or write naming a field absent from that component's schema. The error lists the fields that do exist.
  • A reads_all / writes_all naming an unregistered component.

It does not check for cycles, because a cycle cannot occur. An edge is only recorded when the source index is lower than the target index.

Rusta typo in a field name is a configuration error
let pipeline = Pipeline::new("etl")
    .component::<Transaction>()
    .system(system_fn(
        SystemMeta::new("convert").writes_named("Transaction", "usd_ammount"),
        |_: &mut Dataset| Ok(()),
    ));

let err = pipeline.validate().unwrap_err();
// Configuration: Pipeline: declared access for field 'Transaction.usd_ammount',
// but that field does not exist in the component's schema.
// Known fields: id, amount, currency, valid, usd_amount

Once the plan exists you can read it back. Stages are buckets of system indices, ascending within each bucket, in the order you registered them:

Rustthe plan from the diagram above
pipeline.validate()?;

assert_eq!(pipeline.plan()?, [vec![0, 1], vec![2], vec![3]]);
assert_eq!(pipeline.plan()?.len(), 3);

plan() returns the stages, or the error that building them hit. Adding a component, a schema or a system through component, schema, system, parallel_system, system_boxed or parallel_system_boxed clears the cache, so the next call re-derives everything.

The plan is pinned to the first schema registry it sees

Nothing else invalidates it. Registering a component through data_mut(), inserting a resource, or attaching a source does not clear the cache, and run_on passes the foreign dataset's registry to a slot that is already filled. Whichever dataset triggered the first build is the one every later run is validated and expanded against.

run, run_on, run_stream

Three entry points over the same stage executor. Each returns the RunStats of that call.

CallReceiverOperates onReturns
run()&mut selfits own dataset, plus attached sources and sinksSaciResult<RunStats>
run_on(data)&selfa dataset you pass inSaciResult<RunStats>
run_stream()&mut selfone source batch at a time, through every stage and sinkSaciResult<RunStats>

run_on is the shared-template path: it takes &self, ignores any sources and sinks, and leaves self.data untouched. One pipeline value can therefore be the plan for many independent batches, which is exactly how the distributed runner and the WASM processor apply a template to per-partition datasets.

Rustone plan, many batches
let template = Pipeline::new("processor")
    .component::<Transaction>()
    .system(ValidateSystem)
    .system(EnrichSystem);

for mut batch in incoming_batches {
    let stats = template.run_on(&mut batch).await?;
    tracing::info!(rows = stats.rows_produced, "batch done");
}

With sources or sinks attached, run() drains every source into the dataset, runs the stages, then writes each component to its sink and calls finish() on each. With nothing attached it runs the stages alone. saci ships the Source / Sink traits. FileSource (connector-file) moves bytes, CsvCodec (codec-csv) turns them into batches. See Sources & Sinks.

RunStats

RunStats is a four-field Copy struct that every run call returns for that call alone.

FieldTypeMeaning
rows_producedisizeNet change in live rows across the call. Negative when systems soft-deleted more rows than they appended.
systems_runusizeSystems that executed. Counts a system once no matter how many attempts it took.
elapsedDurationWall clock for the call, retry sleeps included.
retriesu32Failed attempts that were followed by another attempt, summed over every system in every stage.
Rustafter a run
let stats: RunStats = pipeline.run().await?;
println!(
    "{} systems, {:+} rows, {} retries, {} ms",
    stats.systems_run,
    stats.rows_produced,
    stats.retries,
    stats.elapsed.as_millis(),
);

Per-system retry

Every system carries a RetryMode, returned by its retry() method (default RetryMode::None) and snapshotted into the plan alongside the stage buckets. The stage executor never calls a system directly. It hands the call to a retry driver, which counts attempts, sleeps between them, and reports how many retries it consumed. Only an error whose SaciError::is_retryable() is true is retried.

the one moment writes reach the Dataset system attempts, backoff, retry accounting

Three modes, and their arithmetic. n is the zero-based retry number, so the first wait uses n = 0.

ModeAttemptsWait before retry n
None1none
Fixed { retries, delay }retries + 1delay, constant
ExponentialBackoff { .. }max_retries + 1base_delay * multiplier^n, clamped to max_delay, then multiplied by 1 ± jitter

RetryMode::default() is None, so a system that does not override retry() runs once. RetryMode::exponential(3) is ExponentialBackoff with max_retries: 3, base_delay: 100 ms, multiplier: 2.0, max_delay: 30 s, jitter: 0.1. It gives the four attempts and the 100 / 200 / 400 ms waits in the diagram, each scattered by up to ten percent.

Rustoverriding the default for one system
use std::time::Duration;

#[async_trait]
impl System for CallPricingApi {
    fn meta(&self) -> SystemMeta {
        SystemMeta::new("call_pricing_api").writes(Transaction::USD_AMOUNT)
    }

    fn retry(&self) -> RetryMode {
        // Two retries, 50 ms apart, no backoff.
        RetryMode::fixed(2, Duration::from_millis(50))
    }

    async fn run(&self, data: &mut Dataset) -> SaciResult<()> {
        // ...
        Ok(())
    }
}

A failure under RetryMode::None, or an error that is not retryable, returns the original error unwrapped. is_retryable() is true for SystemExecution, Store, RetryExhausted and, with the distributed feature, Distributed and LeaseExpired. SaciError::RetryExhausted { attempts } means the budget was spent after at least one retry, and its source() is the last error.

Two waiting strategies, one counter. Sequential systems retry through run_with_retries, which waits with tokio::time::sleep. An all-parallel stage of two or more systems that clears the row threshold dispatches each system onto a blocking thread, where the driver is run_with_retries_blocking and the wait is std::thread::sleep. Processor builds compiled without the engine feature have no async timer, so delays are skipped there and retries fire immediately. Either path lands its retry counts in the same total.

A retry is observable. Under the tracing feature both drivers open an info-level task_attempt span carrying attempt and max_attempts, but only from the second attempt on. A call that succeeds first try opens none, so a clean run shows no task_attempt at all. Both warn on each failure that will be retried with attempt, max_attempts and delay_ms, and log an error when the budget runs out. See Tracing.

When a system fails

An error that survives its retry budget aborts the whole call. What survives in the dataset depends on the kind of stage it happened in.

  • A stage that runs one at a time, because a plain System is in it or because it sits under the row threshold, stops at the first error. Systems earlier in the stage keep their writes, later systems in that stage never run, and no later stage runs either.
  • A concurrently dispatched stage, meaning all-parallel with two or more members over the row threshold, spawns one task per system and awaits every one of them before inspecting any result. A failing system does not cancel its siblings, and they all burn their own retry budgets. The merged WriteSet is applied only if every task succeeded, which makes that stage all-or-nothing.
  • Either way, the call returns the error and no RunStats.
  • Under run() with sinks attached, sinks are never written and finish() is never called.
Retries re-run against a partly-mutated dataset

A sequential System takes &mut Dataset and writes directly. There is no rollback, so a system that fails after appending rows or applying a WriteSet is retried on top of its own partial work. Make retryable systems idempotent. A ParallelSystem helps only in the stage-atomic case. Its WriteSet is held back until the whole stage succeeds, when that stage was dispatched concurrently. A lone ParallelSystem, one sharing a stage with a plain System, and one in a stage under the row threshold all have their WriteSet applied as soon as they return.
